Yes, as long as the struct is declared volatile
Only if each field is written in address order
why: Each field may be atomic, but the struct as a whole is several accesses. A reader in the middle sees new x with old y: tearing at the struct level.

q: A global uint32_t is written only by an ISR and only read by main(). What does it need?
choices: A critical section, but no volatile
Both volatile and a critical section
Neither, because it is one word
why: volatile makes main() really reload it each time. It needs no critical section: one aligned word with one writer can't tear.

q: A shared uint8_t is written only by the ISR and only read by main(). Does it need a critical section?
choices: No: a single aligned byte access with one writer can't be split
Yes: anything shared with an ISR needs one
Yes: bytes are read as part of a 32-bit word
No, but only if the ISR runs at priority 0
why: A byte is one access, and with only one writer there is nothing to interleave. It still needs volatile so main() really reads it.

q: How many NVIC priority levels does this chip have, and which is most urgent?
why: Only the top 2 bits of each 8-bit priority field exist, giving 4 levels. In the NVIC a lower number is more urgent.

q: Which byte value sets an IRQ to NVIC priority 3?
why: Only bits 7:6 of the byte exist, so the value is prio << 6 = 3 << 6 = 0xC0. Writing 0x03 lands in bits that don't exist.

q: An IRQ's priority byte reads 0x80. What priority level is it?
why: The level is the top two bits: 0x80 = 1000 0000, so bits 7:6 = 10 = 2. Only those two bits are implemented.

q: Code writes 0x03 straight into IRQ 4's priority byte, meaning 'least urgent'. What level does IRQ 4 actually get?
why: The low six bits don't exist and read as 0, so 0x03 becomes 0x00: level 0, the most urgent. The value needs shifting: 3 << 6 = 0xC0.

q: IRQ 2 is given priority 1 and every other IRQ in IPR[0] is 0. What does IPR[0] read?
why: IRQ 2 is byte 2 of IPR[0] (bits 23:16). Its value is 1 << 6 = 0x40, so 0x40 << 16 = 0x00400000. 0x00004000 would be IRQ 1's byte.

q: A timer handler is running when a more urgent interrupt arrives. What happens?
choices: The urgent one preempts the timer handler, which resumes afterwards
The urgent one waits until the timer handler returns
The timer handler is aborted and its work discarded
Both handlers run at once on the same core
why: The NVIC lets a more urgent interrupt preempt a running handler. That also means sharing is now ISR versus ISR, not only ISR versus main().

q: Why must interrupt handlers be short?
choices: A slow handler delays every interrupt of equal or lower priority
Handlers longer than 32 instructions corrupt the stacked frame
The NVIC aborts any handler that runs over 1 ms
Long handlers stop main() from using volatile
why: While a handler runs, equal and lower-priority interrupts wait. The usual shape is: set a flag or buffer the data, return, and let main() do the work.

q: What is priority inversion?
choices: A high-priority task waits, in effect, on a lower-priority one
Priority 0 being most urgent instead of priority 3
Two interrupts with equal priority firing at once
A handler lowering its own priority to finish sooner
why: In priority inversion an urgent task is stuck waiting on something a low-priority task holds. It is introduced in lesson 03 and covered fully in lesson 07.

q: Which famous system kept resetting because of priority inversion?
why: Mars Pathfinder kept resetting on the surface of Mars in 1997 because of priority inversion. Ariane 5 failed from an overflow, and Therac-25 from a race in its software.

q: Suppose a chip implemented the top 3 bits of each priority byte instead of 2. How many priority levels would it have?
why: n implemented bits give 2^n levels: 2 bits give this chip's 4, and 3 bits would give 8. The count doubles per bit; it does not go up by 2.

q: IRQ 0 gets priority 1 and IRQ 1 gets priority 2; IRQs 2 and 3 are left at 0. What does IPR[0] read?
why: IRQ 0 is byte 0: 1 << 6 = 0x40. IRQ 1 is byte 1: 2 << 6 = 0x80, shifted 8 bits to 0x8000. Together that is 0x00008040; 0x00004080 swaps the two bytes.

choices: link.ld: where everything goes; startup.c: what runs first
link.ld: what runs first; startup.c: where everything goes
link.ld: the clock setup; startup.c: the memory map
link.ld: the C library; startup.c: the board pins
why: The linker script decides the layout. startup.c holds the vector table and the code that makes RAM match C's promises before main().

q: Which file holds the vector table, as a C array?
why: The table is a C array in startup.c. link.ld only pins its section, .isr_vector, at the start of flash.

q: Where is flash on the STM32C031C6, and how big is it?
why: Flash is 32 KB at 0x08000000, not at 0. SRAM is the 12 KB region at 0x20000000.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Where is SRAM on the STM32C031C6, and how big is it?
why: SRAM is 12 KB at 0x20000000, so its top is 0x20003000. The 0x20000000 base is the same on every Cortex-M.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Code copied from an STM32F4 tutorial puts GPIOA in the 0x40000000 peripheral region. What is true on this STM32C0?
choices: GPIO sits at 0x50000000 on its own port, so the copied address is wrong
GPIOA is at 0x40020000 on every STM32 family
Both addresses work, because the GPIO block is mirrored into both regions
The compiler rejects addresses outside the CMSIS header
why: On the C0 the I/O ports are outside the peripheral region, at 0x50000000. Copied F4 addresses write somewhere else, and the chip gives no error.

q: GPIO ports are 0x400 apart, starting at GPIOA = 0x50000000. What is GPIOD's base?

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: ODR is at offset 0x14 in every GPIO port. What is the address of GPIOB->ODR?
why: GPIOB's base is 0x50000400, so ODR is at 0x50000400 + 0x14 = 0x50000414. 0x50000014 is GPIOA->ODR.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which base address belongs to USART2?
why: USART2 is 0x40004400. 0x40021000 is RCC, 0x40022000 is FLASH, and 0x50000400 is GPIOB.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which base address belongs to the NVIC?
why: The NVIC is at 0xE000E100 in the core region. 0xE000E010 is SysTick, 0xE000ED00 is the SCB, and 0x40021800 is EXTI.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Code reads an address in the 4 GB space where nothing is mapped. What happens?
choices: It reads the nearest RAM word
why: Addressability is not memory. With only 32 KB and 12 KB inside 4 GB, most addresses are nothing, and reading one is a fault, not a zero.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: 12 KB of RAM is how many bytes in hex?
why: 12 × 1024 = 12 288 = 0x3000, which is why the top of RAM is 0x20000000 + 0x3000 = 0x20003000. 0x1200 is the decimal-looking mistake.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What is CMSIS?
choices: Headers: #defines and structs that name addresses
ST's HAL library, linked into every build
A bootloader that runs before Reset_Handler
A compiled library of driver functions from ARM
why: CMSIS is headers, not a library: nothing is linked and nothing is called. It is not ST's HAL, which is a real library.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which header comes from ARM and covers the NVIC, SysTick and SCB?
why: core_cm0plus.h is ARM's core header. stm32c031xx.h is ST's device header for every peripheral on this part; the HAL is a separate library.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Compared with *(volatile uint32_t *)0x50000014 ^= 1u << 5, what does GPIOA->ODR ^= 1u << 5 compile to?
choices: Smaller code: base in a register, constant offset
Larger code: CMSIS calls an accessor function for every register access
The same code, but it runs more slowly
Larger code: one literal pool entry per register
why: GPIOA->ODR is base + offset computed at compile time, so one base register serves every register. The raw address needs its own literal: 16 bytes against 14.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What does a peripheral do if its RCC clock gate is still off?
choices: Reads back zero and ignores writes, with no error
Raises a HardFault on the first access
Works, but at the 12 MHz reset clock
Holds the last values written before reset
why: An unclocked peripheral is silently deaf: writes vanish and reads return 0. That is why the gate is enabled first, always.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: In RCC->IOPENR, which bits are GPIOAEN and GPIOBEN?
why: IOPENR has one bit per GPIO port, starting with GPIOAEN at bit 0 and GPIOBEN at bit 1.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which value, OR-ed into RCC->IOPENR, enables the clocks of GPIOA and GPIOC?
why: GPIOA is bit 0 (0x1) and GPIOC is bit 2 (0x4), so 0x1 | 0x4 = 0x5. 0x3 enables A and B.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: USART2EN is bit 17 of RCC->APBENR1. Which value enables it?
why: 1u << 17 = 0x00020000. 0x00010000 is bit 16, and 0x00000011 is 17 written in hex by mistake.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which RCC register holds the clock gates of USART2, TIM3 and I2C1?
why: APBENR1 covers USART2, TIM3, I2C1 and others. APBENR2 covers TIM1, SPI1, USART1 and the ADC; IOPENR is the GPIO ports.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: IOPENR is at offset 0x34 in RCC (base 0x40021000). What is its address?
why: 0x40021000 + 0x34 = 0x40021034. The lesson checks this with a _Static_assert against ST's header.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What does the Cortex-M core do at reset, before running any instruction?
choices: Loads word 0 into SP and word 1 into PC
Jumps to address 0 with SP undefined
Calls SystemInit() to start the 48 MHz clock
why: The hardware reads the first two words of the vector table itself: word 0 is the initial SP, word 1 the reset handler. Copying .data is the reset handler's job.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Why can Reset_Handler be written in C here, when an AVR's reset code has to be assembly?
choices: The core loads SP before the first instruction, so a stack exists
The Cortex-M compiler has a special 'reset' keyword
The AVR has no C compiler that is able to emit any startup code at all
Reset_Handler runs only after main() has set the stack
why: C needs a stack. On Cortex-M the hardware loads SP from word 0 before anything runs; on AVR reset just jumps to 0 with no stack set up.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What does section(".isr_vector") do for the vector table array?
choices: Stops the compiler deleting the unused array
Puts the array in flash instead of RAM
Marks every entry as a weak symbol
why: A section of its own lets the linker script place the array at the very start of flash. 'used' stops deletion and 'const' keeps it in flash.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Why does the vector table carry the 'used' attribute?
choices: No C code reads it, so the compiler would delete it
It forces the table to be placed at 0x08000000
It makes each handler entry a strong symbol that overrides the weak alias
It keeps the table out of the .bss section
why: Nothing in your program mentions vectors; only the hardware reads it. Without 'used' the compiler may drop it as dead.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: The const is removed from the vector table declaration. What changes?
choices: It lands in RAM, wasting RAM on a table that never changes
Nothing: arrays of function pointers always go in flash
The build fails, since handlers cannot be in RAM
why: const is what puts the table in flash. Without it, the 180-byte table takes RAM from your 12 KB for no reason.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What is entry 0 of the vector table?
choices: The initial stack pointer, cast to look like a function pointer
The address of Reset_Handler with the Thumb bit set
The address of Default_Handler, as a fallback
A checksum of the rest of the table
why: Entry 0 is &_estack, the initial SP, not a function. The cast lets the whole table be one array. Reset_Handler is entry 1.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which vector number is SysTick?
why: Core entries: 0 SP, 1 Reset, 2 NMI, 3 HardFault, 11 SVCall, 14 PendSV, 15 SysTick. 16 is the first peripheral IRQ (IRQ 0).

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which vector number is HardFault?
why: 0 is the initial SP, 1 Reset, 2 NMI and 3 HardFault.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: At what address is the vector for peripheral IRQ 10?

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: At what address is the HardFault vector?
why: HardFault is vector 3, and each entry is 4 bytes: 0x08000000 + 3 × 4 = 0x0800000C.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: A vector sits at 0x08000070. Which peripheral IRQ does it belong to?
why: 0x70 = 112 bytes, / 4 = vector 28, and 28 − 16 = IRQ 12. 28 is the vector number, not the IRQ.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: size -A reports .isr_vector as 180 bytes. How many peripheral IRQ entries does the table hold?
why: 180 / 4 = 45 entries. Subtract the 16 core entries and 29 are left: IRQ 0 to IRQ 28, which is what the C031 uses.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: At what address is the SysTick vector?

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: A hex file's first data record starts 00 30 00 20 C5 06 00 08. What is the initial SP?
why: ARM is little-endian, so read the four bytes right to left: 20 00 30 00 = 0x20003000, the top of 12 KB RAM.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Same record: the reset vector bytes are C5 06 00 08. Where does Reset_Handler actually start?
why: Little-endian gives 0x080006C5. Bit 0 is the Thumb bit, not part of the address, so the code is at 0x080006C4.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Another board's image begins 00 20 00 20 D9 01 00 08. What are the initial SP and the reset handler's address?
why: Little-endian words: 0x20002000 (top of an 8 KB RAM) and 0x080001D9. Clear the Thumb bit: the handler is at 0x080001D8.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Every handler address in the vector table is odd. Why?
choices: Bit 0 is the Thumb bit; the core reads it as 'Thumb code'
Handlers are aligned to odd addresses for speed
The linker adds 1 to each entry to mark it as used by the hardware
Odd addresses point into RAM instead of flash
why: Bit 0 of every code address on a Cortex-M is the Thumb bit and must be 1. An even entry faults on the first instruction.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: In the vector table, the NMI and HardFault entries hold the same address. What does this mean?
choices: Both are weak aliases of one Default_Handler
The linker has merged two identical handlers by mistake
The table is corrupt and the chip will not boot
NMI is always routed through the HardFault handler
why: Neither handler was written, so both entries point at the same weak default. Identical words are the sign that nothing overrode them.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: How does your own TIM3_IRQHandler get into the vector table?
choices: A strong function of exactly that name replaces the weak alias at link time
You register it with NVIC_SetVector() at the start of main()
You add its address to the vector table in link.ld
The compiler finds it by the ISR attribute on the function
why: Every handler in startup.c is a weak alias of Default_Handler. An ordinary function with exactly the same name wins at link time: the name is the registration.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What does Default_Handler do?
choices: Returns at once with bx lr
why: Default_Handler is an infinite loop. An interrupt that reaches it hangs the board, which is why a misspelt handler shows up as a hang.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: TIM3_IRQHandler is misspelt TIM3_IrqHandler. What do the build and the board do?
choices: No error, no warning; the first interrupt hangs in Default_Handler
The linker reports a duplicate symbol and stops
The build warns that TIM3_IrqHandler is defined but never used anywhere
It works, because the linker matches names case-insensitively
why: The misspelt function is just unused, and the linker even deletes it as dead code. The weak default stays in the vector and the first interrupt hangs.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: nm Main.elf lists your handler. Which letter shows that your function, not the weak default, is installed?
why: T is a normal (strong) text symbol: yours. W means the weak placeholder is still in place. U is undefined and B is .bss.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: In which order does Reset_Handler do its work?
choices: Zero .bss, call main(), then copy .data in the background
why: RAM is made to match C's promises first (.data copied, .bss zeroed), then the clock, then constructors, then main(), and finally a for(;;).

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Why does Reset_Handler end with for(;;) after calling main()?
choices: There is nothing to return to; returning would run into whatever bytes follow
It waits for the next interrupt to restart main()
The C standard requires an infinite loop after main()
It gives the debugger time to attach before reset
why: On a desktop, returning from main() exits the process. Here there is no OS, so the infinite loop is a wall.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Lab: the .data copy loop is deleted. What does int magic = 0xC0FFEE; read in main()?
choices: 0, because RAM is cleared at reset
It faults on the first read
why: The variable lives in RAM, and only the copy loop puts its initial value there. Without it, it holds leftover RAM contents.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Lab: the .bss zero loop is deleted. Where does a global int frames; start?
choices: At whatever RAM held, maybe different each run
At 0: the C compiler and the C standard guarantee it
At the value stored for it in flash
why: C promises .bss is zero, but on this chip the startup code keeps that promise. .bss has no flash copy, so without the loop it is just leftover RAM.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: extern uint32_t _sdata; is declared for a linker symbol. What is it?
choices: A symbol whose value is an address; no storage exists
A uint32_t variable holding the start of .data
A pointer to .data, set by Reset_Handler
A copy of the first word of .data
why: The linker creates no storage for _sdata; the symbol's value is the address. The declaration only gives &_sdata a type.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: uint32_t n = _edata - _sdata; is written to get the size of .data. What happens?
choices: It compiles cleanly and gives garbage
It gives the size in bytes, as intended
The compiler rejects it: the symbols are not defined
It gives the size in 32-bit words
why: Without &, each name reads the four bytes stored at that address. The rule: a linker symbol is only ever used with &.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: &_sdata = 0x20000000 and &_edata = 0x20000064, both as uint32_t *. What does &_edata - &_sdata give?
why: Pointer subtraction counts elements: 0x64 = 100 bytes, / 4 bytes per uint32_t = 25. 100 would be the byte count.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: How does link.ld get _estack?
choices: The core measures RAM size at reset
Reset_Handler sets it at run time
why: _estack = ORIGIN(RAM) + LENGTH(RAM) is computed by the linker, which is why the SP in the image can be trusted.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: A lab shrinks RAM to LENGTH = 6K. What is _estack now?

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What does >RAM AT> FLASH mean for the .data section?
choices: It lives in RAM and is stored in flash
It lives in flash and is cached in RAM
It is copied from RAM to flash at shutdown
It is placed in whichever region has room
why: An initialised global must survive power-off (flash) and be writable (RAM), so it gets two addresses. LOADADDR(.data) = _sidata gives the flash copy.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Why does the .bss section have no AT> FLASH?
choices: Every byte is zero, so there is nothing to store
It is stored in flash right after the vector table instead
.bss is read-only and lives only in flash
The linker stores it compressed in .rodata
why: Storing hundreds of zeros in flash would be waste. .bss gets only a size, and the startup code writes the zeros.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: In link.ld, what is '.' as in _sdata = .; ?
choices: The location counter: the address reached so far
The size of the section so far
why: The dot is the address the linker has reached. Assigning it to a symbol is how every boundary marker is made.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which way does the stack grow on this chip?
why: The SP starts at _estack (top of RAM) and grows down. _sbrk hands malloc the gap between .bss and the stack.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: size -A shows .data 40, .bss 200, ._user_heap_stack 1024 bytes. How much RAM is used?
why: RAM used = .data + .bss + heap/stack = 40 + 200 + 1024 = 1264 B. 1304 counts .data twice; it is flash that does that.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: size -A shows .isr_vector 180, .text 4000, .rodata 500, .data 40 bytes. About how much flash is used?
why: Flash = vectors + .text + .rodata + .data again = 180 + 4000 + 500 + 40 = 4720 B. Leaving out .data gives the tempting 4680.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: In the lesson's own build, .data is 100, .bss 372 and the heap/stack reservation 1536 bytes. How much RAM does the linker report?
why: 100 + 372 + 1536 = 2008 B. The heap and stack reservation is three quarters of that.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which global costs both flash and RAM?
why: An initialised global is in .data: stored in flash and copied to RAM. const goes to .rodata (flash only), and zero-initialised globals go to .bss (RAM only).

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Where does const char msg[] = "hi"; live?
why: const data never changes, so it stays in flash and is read with ordinary ldr. That is why the course says prefer const.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Where does a global int total; (no initialiser) live?
choices: The heap, allocated on first use
why: It is zero-initialised, so it is .bss: RAM only, zeroed by Reset_Handler, and costs no flash.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What clock does the STM32C0 run at straight out of reset?
why: The chip wakes on its 48 MHz internal oscillator divided by four: 12 MHz. SystemInit() changes the divider to ÷1.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What does SystemInit() do, in order?
choices: Set one flash wait state and wait; clear HSIDIV; wait for HSIRDY; set SystemCoreClock
Clear HSIDIV; wait for HSIRDY; then set one flash wait state
Start the PLL; wait for lock; switch the clock source to the PLL
Set SystemCoreClock; then copy .data; then zero .bss
why: The wait state goes up first, then the divider goes to ÷1. The C0 needs no PLL, lock bit or source switch.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: You are lowering the clock from 48 MHz back to 12 MHz. When do you remove the flash wait state?
choices: At the same moment, in one register write
Never: wait states only go up
why: Rule: wait states go up before the frequency and come down after it. The flash must always be slow enough for the current clock.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: SystemInit() switches to 48 MHz before setting the flash wait state. What is the symptom?
choices: The CPU fetches before flash is ready and hangs somewhere unrelated
A clear HardFault pointing at SystemInit()
The chip just keeps running at 12 MHz
why: Flash can't keep up at 48 MHz without the wait state, so instructions are fetched wrong. The part hangs with no error, far from the real bug.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which register holds the flash wait states (LATENCY)?
why: LATENCY is in FLASH->ACR, at 0x40022000. RCC->CR holds HSIDIV and HSIRDY.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What does the C library call to print a character from printf on this board?
choices: putchar(), provided by the startup code
An OS system call, through SVC
why: newlib calls _write(fd, buf, len), and retarget.c implements it by polling USART2. Implement it and printf, puts and putchar all work.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: How does retarget.c send one byte?
choices: Wait for TXE in USART2->ISR, then write TDR
Write TDR, then wait for TXE
Start a DMA transfer to USART2
Set the USART2 interrupt and return
why: It polls: wait while the transmit register is full, then store the byte in TDR.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What USART2 BRR value gives 115 200 baud at 48 MHz?
why: BRR = f / baud = 48 000 000 / 115 200 = 416.7, rounded to the nearest: 417. Truncating gives 416.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: BRR is set to 417 for 48 MHz, but the clock was never raised and the chip still runs at 12 MHz. What happens on the serial line?
choices: Garbage: the real baud is about 28 800, a quarter of 115 200
Nothing changes: the UART has its own 48 MHz clock
It works, but four times faster: about 460 800 baud
The UART refuses to start and TXE never sets
why: Baud = clock / BRR = 12 000 000 / 417 ≈ 28 800, a quarter of what the terminal expects. BRR is only right if the chip really runs at 48 MHz.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: What BRR value gives 38 400 baud at 48 MHz?

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: _sbrk() is broken. What does printf do?
why: _sbrk hands malloc, and printf's buffer, the gap between .bss and the stack. If it fails, printf prints nothing from a program that otherwise runs.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: On the Nucleo-C031C6, where is the user LED LD4?
why: LD4 is on PA5 (also header D13). PA2 is USART2 TX, and PB0–PB7 drive the LED bar.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which pins and alternate function carry USART2 TX and RX?
choices: PA2 TX, PA3 RX, both AF1
PA3 TX, PA2 RX, both AF1
PA2 TX, PA3 RX, both AF7
PA9 TX, PA10 RX, both AF1
why: USART2 is PA2 (TX) and PA3 (RX), alternate function 1 on both. AF7 is the number used on the F4 family.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Which block is on Wokwi's 'not modelled' list?
why: Wokwi doesn't model DMA, RTC, IWDG, PWR, SYSCFG or DBG. On the C0, EXTICR is in EXTI, not SYSCFG, so the interrupt lesson still works.

chapter: Lesson 04 · Startup and the Linker Script
q: Lab 3: .isr_vector is moved after .text in link.ld. What happens?
choices: It builds with no warning and a valid hex file, but the chip can't start
The linker stops with an overlap error
It builds, and the chip boots normally
The hex file fails its checksum and won't load
why: The hardware reads the first two words of flash as SP and PC. They are now instruction bytes, but every automated check still passes.

q: In the course's peripheral model, which slot does EXTI fill for GPIO?
choices: Events: a separate block, not part of GPIO
Control: it is GPIO's mode register
Data in: it latches the IDR register on every pin edge
Clock gate: it powers the GPIO ports
why: GPIO itself does not interrupt. Edges are turned into interrupt requests by a separate block, EXTI.

q: Which GPIO register is the 'data in' slot?
why: IDR reads the pin levels and is read-only. ODR, BSRR and BRR are data out, and PUPDR is control.

q: What is 0xEB in binary?
why: One hex digit is exactly 4 bits: E = 1110, B = 1011. Read them in order, left digit first.

q: GPIOA->MODER resets to 0xEBFFFFFF. What are bits 27:26 (PA13's field)?
why: The second hex digit, B = 1011, covers bits 27:24. Bits 27:26 are its top two, 10: alternate function, the SWD line.

q: Which C expression clears the bits that are 1 in mask and leaves the rest of x alone?
why: AND with the inverted mask zeroes exactly the mask's bits. x | mask sets them instead, and x & mask keeps only them.

q: x = 0xFF. What is x & ~0x0C (8-bit)?
why: ~0x0C = 1111 0011 = 0xF3, and 0xFF & 0xF3 = 0xF3. Only bits 3:2 were cleared.

q: What is the offset of BSRR in a GPIO port?
why: Offsets: IDR 0x10, ODR 0x14, BSRR 0x18, LCKR 0x1C, AFR 0x20/0x24, BRR 0x28.

q: What is the offset of PUPDR in a GPIO port?
why: MODER 0x00, OTYPER 0x04, OSPEEDR 0x08, PUPDR 0x0C. Every port uses the same offsets.

q: What do the four MODER codes mean?
why: MODER: 00 input, 01 output, 10 alternate function, 11 analog. Analog is also the reset state of most pins.

q: In PUPDR, what does the code 10 mean?
why: PUPDR codes: 00 none, 01 pull-up, 10 pull-down, 11 reserved.

q: What does OTYPER bit n = 1 select for pin n?
why: OTYPER is one bit per pin: 0 push-pull (the reset value), 1 open-drain.

q: What does LCKR do?
choices: Freezes a pin's configuration until reset
Locks the output level of a pin
Blocks every interrupt coming from that port's pins
why: LCKR freezes the configuration registers of the chosen pins until the next reset. The lessons don't use it.

q: Which bits of GPIOB->MODER belong to PB3, and what value makes it an output?
why: MODER has 2 bits per pin at 2n+1:2n, so n = 3 gives bits 7:6. Output is 01; 10 would be alternate function.

q: Which PUPDR bits belong to PA12?
why: PUPDR is 2 bits per pin: 2 × 12 + 1 : 2 × 12 = 25:24.

q: PA9 needs alternate function 1. Which register and bits hold its AF number?
why: AFR[9 / 8] = AFR[1]; 9 mod 8 = 1, so bits 4·1+3 : 4·1 = 7:4. Write 0001 there.

q: Which register and bits hold pin 14's alternate-function number?
why: 14 / 8 = 1, so AFR[1]; 14 mod 8 = 6, so bits 27:24. AFR[0] bits 27:24 belong to pin 6.

q: Which BSRR bit drives pin 7 low?
why: In BSRR, bit n sets and bit n + 16 resets: 7 + 16 = 23.

q: Which GPIOA pins do not wake in analog mode, and why?
choices: PA13 and PA14: they are the SWD debug lines
PA0 and PA1: they are wired to the two user buttons
PA2 and PA3: they carry USART2
PA5 only: it drives the user LED
why: Every pin resets to 11 (analog) except PA13 and PA14, which reset to 10 (alternate function) so a debugger can reach the chip.

q: An active-low button's pin is never set to input mode. What does the program see?
choices: 'Pressed' forever: an analog pin reads 0 in IDR
Random presses: the analog pin floats and drifts between levels
'Released' forever: the pull-up holds it at 1
Correct readings: input is the reset mode
why: Pins wake analog, and an analog pin reads 0 in IDR whatever the voltage. Active low means 0 = pressed. Input mode must be written, never assumed.

q: PUPDR resets to 0x24000000. What pull does PA14 have?
why: 0x2 = 0010 is bits 31:28, so PA14 (bits 29:28) is 10, pull-down. The 4 = 0100 gives PA13 (bits 27:26) = 01, pull-up.

q: OSPEEDR resets to 0x0C000000. What does that mean?
choices: PA13 is very high speed; every other pin very low
PA2 and PA3 are very high speed
Every pin is very high speed except PA13
PA14 and PA15 are very low speed
why: 0x0C000000 has only bits 27:26 = 11, PA13's field: the debug clock line. All other fields are 00, very low.

q: What can an open-drain output do?
choices: Drive low, or let go so a pull-up makes the high
Drive high and low, like push-pull
Drive high only, with a pull-down for the low
Only read the pin, never drive it
why: Open-drain uses only the N-MOS: it pulls low or lets go. The high has to come from a resistor.

q: Two outputs share one wire; one drives high and the other low. When is that a short?
choices: When either has a pull-up enabled
why: Two push-pull outputs fighting connect 3.3 V to ground through two transistors. Open-drain outputs can share a wire; at worst both pull low.

q: Several open-drain outputs share one wire with a pull-up. What logic does the wire compute?
choices: Wired-AND: it is 1 only if every output lets go
Wired-OR: the wire is 1 if any one output drives it high
why: Any output pulling low makes the wire 0, so it is 1 only when all let go. This is how I²C puts many chips on two wires.

q: What does OSPEEDR control?
choices: The slope of each output edge
How often software can toggle the pin
The input sampling rate of IDR
why: Speed is how sharply the output switches, not the toggle rate. Faster edges radiate more noise, so choose the slowest that works.

q: A button connects a pin to GND when pressed. What does the pin need, and what does it read when pressed?
choices: A pull-up; it reads 0 when pressed
A pull-down; it reads 1 when pressed
A pull-up; it reads 1 when pressed
No resistor; it reads 0 when pressed
why: Released, the pull-up makes the pin 1; pressed, the switch pulls it to 0. That is active low.

q: An input pin with no pull resistor is connected to a released button. What does IDR show?
choices: A random level: the pin floats
The last level that was written to ODR for that pin
why: A pin connected to nothing drifts and reads randomly. That is the 'phantom presses' symptom of a missing pull-up.

q: GPIOA->IDR reads 0x00000024. What is (GPIOA->IDR >> 2) & 1u?
why: 0x24 = 0010 0100: bits 5 and 2 are set. Shifting right by 2 brings bit 2 to bit 0, and & 1 keeps it: 1.

q: Starting from reset (0xEBFFFFFF), what does GPIOA->MODER read after the clear-then-set that makes PA5 an output?
why: Clear bits 11:10: 0xEBFFFFFF & 0xFFFFF3FF = 0xEBFFF3FF. OR in 1 << 10 = 0x400: 0xEBFFF7FF. 0xEBFFF3FF is input (00); 0xEBFFFBFF is AF (10).

q: From reset (0xEBFFFFFF), what does MODER read after making PA6 an output with clear-then-set?
why: PA6 is bits 13:12, mask 0x3000. Clearing gives 0xEBFFCFFF; OR 1 << 12 = 0x1000 gives 0xEBFFDFFF.

q: From reset (0xEBFFFFFF), what does MODER read after setting PA4 to alternate function (10)?
why: PA4 is bits 9:8. Clear: 0xEBFFFCFF. OR 2 << 8 = 0x200: 0xEBFFFEFF. 0xEBFFFDFF would be output (01).

q: Code writes GPIOA->MODER = 1u << 10; to make PA5 an output. What else happens?
choices: Every other pin becomes input, including the debug pins
The write is ignored because MODER is read-only
why: A plain assignment writes the whole register, 0x00000400: 00 (input) for every other pin, PA13/PA14 included. Clear-then-set changes only bits 11:10.

q: Code writes GPIOA->MODER |= 1u << 10; on a pin at its reset value. What mode does PA5 end in?
choices: Input: OR clears the other bit
why: OR can only turn bits on, never off. The field was 11, so it stays 11. The clear step is required.

q: GPIOA->PUPDR reads 0x24000000. What does it read after enabling a pull-up on PA4 with clear-then-set?
why: PA4's field is bits 9:8. Clearing leaves 0x24000000; OR 1 << 8 = 0x100 gives 0x24000100. 0x24000200 would be a pull-down.

q: GPIOA->PUPDR reads 0x24000000. What does it read after a pull-down on PA3?
why: PA3's field is bits 7:6, and pull-down is 10: 2 << 6 = 0x80. 0x24000040 would be a pull-up.

q: From PUPDR = 0x24000000, pull-ups are enabled on PA0 and then PA1. Final value?
why: PA0: 01 in bits 1:0 → 0x1. PA1: 01 in bits 3:2 → 0x4. Together 0x5 = 0101. 0x2400000A would be pull-downs.

q: main() does GPIOA->ODR |= 1u << 5 while an ISR does GPIOA->ODR |= 1u << 6. What can go wrong?
choices: The ISR's change is lost if it lands mid read-modify-write
Nothing: ODR writes are atomic on a single-core Cortex-M0+
Both pins toggle instead of being set
The ISR faults because ODR is in use
why: ODR |= is three instructions. If the ISR runs between main()'s ldr and str, main() writes back a stale copy and PA6 goes off again.

q: Why is GPIOA->BSRR = 1u << 5 safe against an ISR that also changes port A?
choices: It is one store, so it is atomic
BSRR masks interrupts while it is written
BSRR is declared volatile in CMSIS
why: There is nothing to read and nothing stale to write back. An interrupt can land before or after the one store, never inside it.

q: What does writing a 0 to a bit of BSRR do?
why: In BSRR a 0 means 'leave alone'. Only a 1 at bit n (set) or bit n + 16 (reset) changes a pin.

q: Which single line drives PA5 low without touching any other pin?
why: Bit 5 + 16 = 21 is PA5's reset bit. 1u << 5 sets it high, writing 0 does nothing, and ODR has no bit 21 for this.

q: Which single BSRR value sets PB1 high and PB6 low and leaves every other pin of port B alone?
Which BSRR value sets PA3 high and drives PA8 low?
The LED bar uses GPIOB->BSRR = ((uint32_t)(uint8_t)~leds << 16) | leds;. What is written for leds = 0x0F?
why: Low half: 0x0F sets PB0–PB3. ~0x0F as 8 bits is 0xF0, shifted to the reset half: PB4–PB7 off. PB8–PB15 stay untouched.

q: What does GPIOA->BRR = 1u << 5 do?
why: BRR (offset 0x28) is BSRR's reset half on its own: bit n resets pin n. It is write-only and atomic too.

q: MODER = 10 on a pin. What does AFR add?
choices: Whether the pin is push-pull or open-drain
why: MODER = 10 says a peripheral owns the pin; AFR's 4-bit number says which. Neither alone is enough.

q: Where does the AF number for USART2 on PA2 come from?
choices: The datasheet's alternate-function table; it differs per pin
It is always AF1 for every UART
The reference manual's register reset values
It equals the peripheral's IRQ number
why: AF numbers are looked up per pin in the datasheet. USART2 on PA2/PA3 is AF1 here, but another pin or chip may differ.

q: A UART pin has MODER = 10 but the wrong AF number. What does the board do?
choices: Looks configured and carries nothing, with no error
Raises a HardFault on the first write
Falls back to the default peripheral for that pin automatically
Sends data at the wrong baud rate
why: The wrong AF just connects some other peripheral, or nothing. No fault, no error, just a silent pin.

q: PA9 and PA10 are both set to AF1. Assuming AFR[1] started at 0, what does it read?
why: PA9 is AFR[1] bits 7:4 and PA10 bits 11:8, each 0001: 0x00000110. 0x00001100 is AFR[0] with PA2 and PA3 on AF1.

q: In which order does gpio_init() set up a pin?
why: Every peripheral follows clock, configure, use. Without the clock first, every configuration write vanishes.

q: The code configures MODER and writes ODR correctly but never sets RCC->IOPENR for the port. What happens?
choices: Writes vanish and reads return 0, with no error
The LED works, but at a lower speed
A HardFault on the first MODER write
The compiler warns that the RCC clock gate was never set
why: An unclocked port is silently deaf. Both pieces of code look correct, and the LED stays dark.

q: Roughly how does a typical button press bounce?
why: Contacts hit, bounce apart and hit again for about a millisecond. Wokwi models 10 to 100 transitions per press.

q: How does lesson 05's debouncer decide a new level is real?
choices: It is unchanged for DEBOUNCE_MS samples in a row
It appears in the majority of the last 20 samples
It appears at least once in the last 20 ms
It is confirmed by an EXTI edge
why: The level must hold for DEBOUNCE_MS (20) consecutive 1 ms samples. Any change restarts the count.

q: DEBOUNCE_MS = 20, samples every 1 ms. A press bounces, and the last bounce is at t = 3 ms. When is the press reported?
why: Every change restarts the count, so the event comes DEBOUNCE_MS after the last bounce: 3 + 20 = 23 ms.

q: DEBOUNCE_MS = 4, 1 ms samples, 'stable' starts at 0. Raw samples from ms 1: 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 … At which ms is the press reported?
why: The last change is at ms 6. Four more equal samples (ms 7, 8, 9, 10) bring held to 4, so the press is reported at ms 10. ms 9 is counting the change itself as a sample.

q: Polling the button at 1 kHz reports only 1–2 level changes per press. Why?
choices: Sampling is too slow to see most bounces
The button barely bounces at all
The pull-up resistor filters the bounces out
why: Bounces are microseconds apart, samples a millisecond apart, so most bounces fall between samples. Polling is a filter.

q: What weakness of polling does a slow printf in the main loop expose?
choices: The loop doesn't come back in time, so samples are late or missed
printf disables interrupts while it runs
why: Polling depends on the loop coming back. Anything slow delays the next sample, and a pulse shorter than the loop is invisible.

q: printf sends 23 characters at 115 200 baud (10 bits per character). About how long does the loop stall?
why: One character takes 10 / 115 200 ≈ 87 µs, so 23 characters take 230 / 115 200 ≈ 2.0 ms: two missed 1 ms samples. 87 µs is a single character.

q: What is the full interrupt path for a button edge?
why: EXTI turns the edge into a request, the NVIC enables and ranks it, and the vector table gives the handler's address.

q: What are the EXTICR port codes?
why: Codes are 0 = A, 1 = B, 2 = C, 3 = D, 5 = F. Port F is 5, not 4: code 4 would be port E, which this chip doesn't have.

q: A button on PB6 must interrupt. What goes in EXTICR, assuming the register started at 0?
why: Line 6 is in EXTICR[6 / 4] = EXTICR[1], bits 8·(6 mod 4)+7 : 8·2 = 23:16. Port B's code is 1: 1 << 16 = 0x00010000.

q: PF2 is to raise an EXTI interrupt. What goes into EXTICR[0], assuming it started at 0?
why: Line 2 is bits 23:16 of EXTICR[0], and port F's code is 5: 5 << 16 = 0x00050000. 0x00040000 uses the wrong code 4.

q: PA1 and PB1 both need interrupts. What is true?
choices: They share line 1, so only one of them can interrupt
Both work: each GPIO port has its own separate set of 16 EXTI lines
Both work, but at different NVIC priorities
Only PB1 can, because B outranks A
why: Line n watches pin n of one port only: EXTICR is a multiplexer that picks one input.

q: A button on PA1 works even though the code never writes EXTICR. Moved to PC1, it is dead. Why?
choices: Port A's code is 0, the reset value, so PA1 worked by luck
PC1 has no internal pull-up resistor on this 48-pin package
Port C cannot raise interrupts on this chip
EXTICR is only read once, at reset
why: EXTICR resets to 0, which already selects port A. Every other port must be written explicitly.

q: Where is EXTICR on the STM32C0, compared with the STM32F4?
choices: In EXTI on the C0; in SYSCFG on the F4
In SYSCFG on the C0; in EXTI on the F4
why: On the C0, EXTICR is part of EXTI. F4 code using SYSCFG->EXTICR won't compile here.

q: A button with a pull-up is pressed. Which EXTI trigger register catches the press?
why: Active low: pressing takes the pin from 1 to 0, a falling edge. The release is the rising edge.

q: Which line correctly clears line 1's falling-edge pending flag?
why: Pending bits are write 1 to clear, and writing 0 does nothing. |= would also write back other lines' pending 1s and clear them.

q: FPR1 reads 0x00000012. The handler for line 1 runs EXTI->FPR1 |= 1u << 1;. Which pending flags does that clear?
why: |= reads 0x12 and writes back 0x12 | 0x02 = 0x12, a 1 at bits 1 and 4. Write-1-to-clear clears both, so line 4's edge is lost unhandled.

q: During EXTI setup, when should IMR1 be unmasked?
choices: Last, after edges are set and old pending flags are cleared
Before the edge triggers, after the NVIC
It doesn't matter; IMR1 is ignored until reset
why: If you unmask before clearing stale pending flags, an old edge can fire the handler at once.

q: How does the STM32C0 latch edges compared with older STM32 families?
choices: Separately: RPR1 for rising, FPR1 for falling
In one shared PR register for both edges, like older families
Only in the NVIC's ISPR register
why: The C0 has separate rising and falling pending registers. Older families have a single PR.

q: What does writing 0 to a bit of NVIC ISER do?
why: ISER is set-enable: a 1 enables and a 0 is ignored. You disable an IRQ through ICER.

q: NVIC_EnableIRQ for IRQ 7. What does it write to ISER?
why: Bit n = IRQ n: 1 << 7 = 0x80. Writing 0x07 would enable IRQs 0, 1 and 2.

q: NVIC_SetPriority(IRQ 5, 2). What does IPR[1] read, if the other bytes are 0?
why: IRQ 5 is in IPR[5 / 4] = IPR[1], byte 5 mod 4 = 1 (bits 15:8). The value is 2 << 6 = 0x80, shifted 8: 0x00008000.

q: IRQ 7 is set to priority 1, the rest of IPR[1] is 0. What does IPR[1] read?
why: IRQ 7 is byte 3 of IPR[1] (bits 31:24). The value is 1 << 6 = 0x40, so 0x40 << 24 = 0x40000000.

q: EXTI4_15_IRQn is IRQ 7. What is its vector number, and where is the vector?
objdump shows the bytes a5 03 00 08 in a vector slot. Where does the handler's code start?
why: Little-endian: 0x080003A5. Bit 0 is the Thumb bit, so the function itself (nm's address) is 0x080003A4.

q: Which EXTI lines share IRQ 7?
why: IRQ 5 = lines 0–1, IRQ 6 = lines 2–3, IRQ 7 = lines 4–15. IRQ 7 is not 'line 7'.

q: A button on PB9 is set up for an EXTI interrupt. Which IRQ and handler run?
why: PB9 is on line 9, and lines 4–15 share IRQ 7. There is no per-line handler for line 9.

q: Why must EXTI0_1_IRQHandler read the pending bits?
choices: IRQ 5 is shared by lines 0 and 1, so the vector alone doesn't say which fired
To tell the NVIC to stop pending the IRQ
Reading them is what re-enables interrupts
The handler's own priority is stored there
why: Several lines share one vector, and the IRQ can even be pended by software with nothing in EXTI. Never trust the vector; read the pending bit.

q: The handler forgets to clear the EXTI pending bit. What does the board do after the first press?
choices: 'Freezes': the handler runs again and again
Crashes into HardFault on the second interrupt entry
Counts that press, then ignores later ones
why: The NVIC sees the line as long as the bit is set, so the handler re-enters as soon as it returns. It hasn't crashed: it is running flat out.

q: Why doesn't the handler debounce by waiting 20 ms itself?
choices: It would block everything of equal or lower priority for 20 ms
The NVIC aborts handlers after 1 ms
EXTI loses its pending bits after 1 ms
why: Handlers record; main() decides. The handler counts edges, and main() runs a 20 ms 'quiet' stopwatch.

q: b_edges is incremented in the handler and only read by main(), with no lock. Why is that safe?
choices: One aligned 32-bit word, one writer, and volatile
main() always reads it inside a __disable_irq() critical section
why: A single aligned word written by one side can't tear. volatile makes main() reload it each time.

q: With bounce on, button B (interrupt) shows tens of edges per press, but button A (polled) shows 1–2. Which is right?
choices: Both: the interrupt sees every edge; the poll samples a summary
Only A: the interrupt is double-counting
Only B: the polled code has a bug
Neither: Wokwi's bounce model is wrong
why: An interrupt sees every edge, wanted or not; polling filters. They answer different questions.

q: Edges latch in FPR1, but the NVIC never sees the request and the handler never runs. What was forgotten?
choices: Setting the line's bit in IMR1
Clearing the pending bit in the handler
why: IMR1 is the gate between EXTI and the NVIC. Masked, the edge is recorded in FPR1 but goes no further.

q: The NVIC shows IRQ 5 pending, but the handler never runs. What was forgotten?
why: The request reached the NVIC (it is pending) but the IRQ is not enabled in ISER, so it is held.

q: The board hangs on the first press, and nm shows EXTI0_1_IRQHandler as W. What is the cause?
choices: The pending bit is never cleared
The NVIC priority is too high
The IOPENR clock gate is off
why: W means the weak placeholder is still in vector 21, so the press jumps to Default_Handler and loops. Your misspelt function was deleted as dead code.

q: A released button gives random 'phantom' presses. Which of the seven silences is it?
why: Without a pull-up, the released pin floats and reads randomly. A missing input mode reads 0 instead: 'pressed' forever.

q: Which interrupt bug is the opposite of the seven 'silences'?
choices: Not clearing the pending bit: the handler runs forever
A misspelt handler name that the linker silently replaces
why: The seven give silence. Forgetting to clear the pending bit gives too much: the handler re-enters forever.

q: Which switch in the interrupt path starts out on?
why: Every other switch on the path resets off. PRIMASK resets to 0, so interrupts are globally on.

q: In the debugger, which register write fakes an edge on EXTI line 1 with no button?
why: SWIER1 is EXTI's software trigger: writing 1 at bit n is an edge on line n, and it sets the pending bit. IDR is read-only.

q: IRQ 5 is pended with NVIC->ISPR = 32 and no EXTI edge. What does the handler do?
choices: Enters, finds no pending bit, and counts nothing
Counts one edge, exactly as if the button had been pressed
Hangs, because nothing clears the pending bit
why: The NVIC runs the handler, but RPR1/FPR1 are empty so its if is false. That is correct: never trust the vector, read the pending bit.

q: Where should you put a breakpoint to stop once per real press?
choices: Where the event is decided, e.g. d->stable = raw;
On the first line of debounce_step(), which runs every millisecond
why: b_edges++ stops on every bounce edge, and debounce_step() runs 1000 times a second. Break where the event is decided.

q: Where does SysTick live, and how does that differ from TIM3?
choices: In the ARM core at 0xE000E010, the same on every Cortex-M
In ST's peripheral space at 0x40000400, right beside TIM3
In the NVIC block at 0xE000E100, wired as an ordinary IRQ 15
In ST's RCC block, so its address differs on each STM32 part
why: SysTick is part of the Cortex-M core, at 0xE000E010 on every Cortex-M. That is why every RTOS uses it as a heartbeat. TIM3 is ST silicon at 0x40000400.

q: Which bit of SysTick CTRL is COUNTFLAG?
why: CTRL holds ENABLE (bit 0), TICKINT (bit 1), CLKSOURCE (bit 2) and COUNTFLAG (bit 16). Bit 24 is not a CTRL field; LOAD and VAL use bits 23:0.

q: What does the TICKINT bit of SysTick CTRL do?
choices: Makes each wrap to 0 raise the SysTick exception
Selects the core clock instead of the external one
Starts the counter counting down from LOAD
Records that the counter has wrapped since the last read
why: TICKINT (bit 1) enables the interrupt. ENABLE (bit 0) starts counting, CLKSOURCE (bit 2) picks the clock, and COUNTFLAG (bit 16) is the wrap flag.

q: Which way does SysTick's VAL count, and what does writing VAL do?
choices: Down to 0; any write clears it
Up to LOAD; any write sets it to LOAD
Down to 0; a write loads the value written
why: VAL counts down and any write clears it to 0, whatever value is written. It does not load the written value; LOAD holds the reload value.

q: How wide are SysTick's LOAD and VAL registers?
why: LOAD and VAL use bits 23:0 only, so the longest period is 2²⁴ clocks. The timers TIM3 and TIM14 are the 16-bit ones.

q: SysTick_Config(SystemCoreClock / 1000) at 48 MHz leaves which value in LOAD?
why: LOAD holds period − 1: 48 000 000 / 1000 = 48 000 clocks, so LOAD = 47 999. 48000 is the classic forgotten −1.

q: A 1 ms SysTick tick on a chip still at its 12 MHz reset clock needs which LOAD?
why: 12 000 000 / 1000 = 12 000 clocks per ms, and LOAD = ticks − 1 = 11 999. 47999 is the 48 MHz value.

q: What is the longest SysTick period at 48 MHz?
why: 2²⁴ clocks / 48 MHz ≈ 0.35 s. 1.4 s would be at 12 MHz, 65.5 ms is a 16-bit microsecond timer's wrap, and 49.7 days is the uint32_t millisecond counter's wrap.

q: What value does SysTick_Config() leave in CTRL?
why: CTRL = CLKSOURCE | TICKINT | ENABLE = bits 2, 1, 0 = 0x7. COUNTFLAG is a status bit the hardware sets, not something SysTick_Config writes.

q: Which NVIC priority does SysTick_Config() give SysTick on this chip?
why: It sets (1 << __NVIC_PRIO_BITS) − 1 = 3 with 2 priority bits: the lowest. Time-keeping is rarely the most urgent thing; a late tick is still counted.

q: What must SysTick_Handler do to acknowledge its interrupt?
choices: Nothing: taking the exception acknowledges it
Write 1 to COUNTFLAG to clear the request
Write 0 to COUNTFLAG, the timer convention
Read VAL, which clears the pending request
why: SysTick_Handler has no flag to clear, unlike every other handler in the course; its request is the wrap itself. Inventing a clear for it is the trap.

q: Lesson 05 polled COUNTFLAG to count milliseconds. Why did that clock lose time?
choices: COUNTFLAG remembers only one wrap, so the extra wraps vanish
COUNTFLAG clears itself after 1 µs, before the loop gets to read it
Polling reads VAL, and every read of VAL restarts the count from LOAD
The poll ran at a lower NVIC priority than the printf did
why: COUNTFLAG records only one wrap. While a printf blocks for ~8 ms, seven more wraps happen and only one is remembered. Reading VAL does not reset it; writing does.

q: A polled 1 ms clock is stuck in a printf of 90 characters at 115 200 baud. About how many milliseconds does it lose?
why: 90 bytes × 86.8 µs ≈ 7.8 ms. COUNTFLAG keeps one of the ~8 wraps, so about 7 ms vanish. The interrupt-driven ms_ticks++ loses none.

q: A uint32_t millisecond counter wraps after about how long?
why: 2³² ms ≈ 4.29 × 10⁹ ms ≈ 49.7 days. 65.5 s is a uint16_t millisecond counter; 24.9 days is where a signed int32 turns negative.

q: Which timeout test is correct even when the millisecond counter wraps?
why: Unsigned subtraction is modulo 2³², so now − start is the true elapsed time even across the wrap. Comparing absolute times, as in the other three, breaks on day 50.

q: start = 0xFFFFFF00 and millis() now returns 0x00000100. What is millis() − start, and has a 500 ms timeout expired?
why: 0x100 − 0xFFFFFF00 = 0x200 = 512 modulo 2³², and 512 ≥ 500. Unsigned arithmetic never goes negative.

q: start = 0xFFFFFE00, now = 0x00000100. Elapsed time by now − start?
why: 0x100 − 0xFFFFFE00 = 0x300 = 768: 0x200 (512) before the wrap plus 0x100 (256) after it.

q: start = 0xFFFFFF00 and the code waits with if (millis() >= start + 500). What goes wrong?
choices: start + 500 wraps to 0xF4, so it fires about 16 ms after start
start + 500 overflows to 0, so it never fires
Nothing: it fires at exactly 500 ms
It fires 500 ms late, after the next wrap
why: start + 500 = 0x000000F4 after the wrap. When millis() is 0xFFFFFF10, only 16 ms in, it is already ≥ 0xF4, so the timeout fires ~484 ms early. Only the subtraction form is always right.

q: In the superloop, a job runs when now − ping_at >= 100. Why update with ping_at += 100 rather than ping_at = now?
choices: += keeps jobs on a fixed grid so lateness does not pile up
+= is faster: a single add instead of another call to millis()
= now would overflow the 32-bit counter once 49.7 days have passed
= now makes the job run twice whenever the loop arrives late
why: If a pass runs 3 ms late, = now shifts every later run by 3 ms and the error adds up; += period keeps the 100 ms grid and absorbs the lateness.

q: ping_at = 1000 and the loop notices at now = 1003. With ping_at += 100, when is the next ping due?
why: += 100 gives 1100: back on the 100 ms grid. ping_at = now would have made it 1103, and the 3 ms would stay forever.

q: What is the weakness of lesson 06's cooperative superloop?
choices: One slow job delays every other job
It cannot run more than three jobs
It loses ticks whenever printf blocks
Jobs drift off their grid after 49.7 days
why: A job stops only when it returns, so one 50 ms job delays all the others by 50 ms; a CPU hog freezes everything. Lesson 07's preemptive kernel removes that limit.

q: Which registers form a timer's time base?
why: Time base: PSC, ARR, CNT (how fast, how far). Events: EGR, DIER, SR. Channel: CCMR1, CCER, CCR1. Control: CR1.

q: Which bits of CR1 start a timer and turn on ARR preloading?
choices: CEN starts it; ARPE turns on ARR preload
UG starts it; OC1PE turns on ARR preload
CEN starts it; UIE turns on ARR preload
UE starts it; ARPE turns on ARR preload
why: CR1.CEN runs the counter and CR1.ARPE preloads ARR. UG is in EGR, OC1PE preloads CCR1 (in CCMR1), UIE is an interrupt enable, and UE belongs to the USART.

q: What are the base addresses of TIM3 and TIM14?
why: TIM3 is at 0x40000400 and TIM14 at 0x40002000. 0xE000E010 is SysTick and 0x40004400 is USART2.

q: What is a timer's update frequency?
why: The prescaler divides by PSC + 1, then the counter runs 0 … ARR, which is ARR + 1 counts. Both registers hold N − 1.

q: At 48 MHz, which PSC and ARR give 1 MHz counting and a 20 ms period?
why: 48 MHz / 48 = 1 MHz, so PSC = 47; 20 ms = 20 000 counts, so ARR = 19 999. PSC = 479 with ARR = 1999 gives 20 ms too, but counts at 100 kHz, not 1 MHz.

q: At 48 MHz, choose PSC and ARR for a timer that counts at 1 MHz and updates every 1 ms.
why: 48 MHz / (47 + 1) = 1 MHz, and 1000 counts = 1 ms, so ARR = 999. PSC = 4799 with ARR = 9 is 1 kHz too, but counts at 10 kHz.

q: At 48 MHz, PSC = 47 and ARR = 9999. What is the update rate?
why: 48 000 000 / (48 × 10 000) = 100 Hz: 1 MHz counting, 10 ms per period.

q: At 48 MHz you want the counter to tick every 100 µs (10 kHz). Which PSC?
why: 48 MHz / 10 kHz = 4800, and PSC holds N − 1 = 4799. 479 gives 100 kHz; 47999 gives 1 kHz.

q: At the 12 MHz reset clock, which PSC makes a timer count at 1 MHz?
why: 12 MHz / (11 + 1) = 1 MHz. 47 is the 48 MHz value, and is exactly the bug if the clock is not yet switched up.

q: Someone writes PSC = 48 and ARR = 19999 at 48 MHz, intending 50 Hz. What happens?
choices: It runs at about 49 Hz, and only a cross-check notices
It runs at exactly 50 Hz; the extra 1 is absorbed
It refuses to start, because PSC must be odd
It runs at 25 Hz, because PSC doubles the period
why: 48 MHz / (49 × 20 000) ≈ 48.98 Hz, about 2 % slow. Nothing complains; only the report line's TIM3-versus-SysTick count notices.

q: What value is in TIM3's ARR for a 20 ms frame at 1 MHz, in hex?
why: 19 999 = 0x4E1F. 0x4E20 is 20 000 (forgot the −1), 0x2F is PSC = 47, and 0xBB7F is SysTick's 47 999.

q: TIM3's PSC, ARR and CCR1 are double-buffered. What does that mean for a write?
choices: Writes go to a preload copy and take effect at the next update
It is written twice, so a glitch on one of the copies is corrected
It takes effect at once, and the old value is kept aside as a backup
It is ignored until the timer has been disabled and enabled again
why: Writes land in a preload register; the counter keeps using the shadow copy until the next update. That is what lets a PWM duty change without a malformed pulse.

q: Why write EGR = UG right after setting PSC and ARR?
choices: To force an update now, so the new values take effect
To enable the update interrupt for the very first time after reset
To clear the update flag that was left over from the reset sequence
To start the counter, which setting CEN on its own cannot do
why: UG generates an update event by software, copying the preload registers into the shadows. UIE enables the interrupt, CEN starts the counter, and UG actually sets UIF rather than clearing it.

q: After EGR = UG, the code enables UIE without clearing anything. What happens?
choices: A phantom interrupt fires at once, because UG raised UIF
Nothing: UG clears UIF as part of the update
The timer stays stopped until UIF is cleared
The first real update is skipped instead
why: UG raises UIF like any update. Clear it (SR = ~TIM_SR_UIF) before enabling UIE, or the first interrupt is a phantom.

q: PSC = 47 is written but EGR = UG is skipped; ARR = 19999 took effect at once. How long is TIM3's first period at 48 MHz?
why: The prescaler is still 0 for the first period, so 20 000 counts run at 48 MHz: 20 000 / 48 MHz ≈ 0.42 ms instead of 20 ms.

q: Which line clears only UIF in TIM3_IRQHandler?
why: Timer flags clear by writing 0, and writing 1 leaves a flag alone. ~TIM_SR_UIF writes 0 to UIF and 1 to everything else. TIM_SR_UIF is the EXTI style.

q: TIM3_IRQHandler clears its flag with TIM3->SR = TIM_SR_UIF (the EXTI style). What does the board do?
choices: The handler re-enters forever: UIF stays set
Works normally: writing 1 clears a flag on every STM32 peripheral
HardFaults, because SR is a read-only register
The compiler warns that the clearing convention is the wrong one
why: Writing 1 to UIF leaves it set and writing 0 to every other bit clears them. The handler returns with UIF still pending and runs again forever. It builds with zero warnings.

q: What 32-bit value does TIM3->SR = ~TIM_SR_UIF write (UIF is bit 0)?
why: ~0x00000001 = 0xFFFFFFFE: a 0 in bit 0 clears UIF, 1s everywhere else leave the other flags alone.

q: By lesson 06, how do the three flags seen so far clear?
choices: EXTI: write 1; TIM SR: write 0; CC1IF: read CCR1
EXTI: write 0; TIM SR: write 1; CC1IF: read CCR1
All three clear by writing 1 to the flag
EXTI: read; TIM SR: write 0; CC1IF: write 1
why: Same chip, three conventions. The guide's lesson: for every flag, look up how it clears.

q: In PWM mode 1 (OC1M = 110), when is the pin high?
why: Mode 1 drives the pin high while the count is below CCR1 and low after, until ARR wraps the counter.

q: Why is CCR1 the pulse width in microseconds in this lesson?
choices: The counter ticks once per microsecond (1 MHz)
CCR1 is defined in microseconds by the hardware
The ISR converts CCR1 to microseconds each frame
ARR is 19999, which scales CCR1 to microseconds
why: With PSC = 47 at 48 MHz the counter counts at 1 MHz, so one count is one microsecond and CCR1 = 1500 means 1.5 ms.

q: How involved is the CPU in each PWM edge on PA6?
choices: Not at all; the ISR only changes CCR1
It toggles the pin in the update ISR every edge
It sets the pin at the update and clears it in a compare ISR
It polls CNT and writes BSRR at CCR1
why: The timer drives the pin by itself. The CPU is involved in no edge; the update ISR only moves CCR1.

q: Which four things turn on TIM3 channel 1 PWM output on a pin?
choices: CCMR1 mode + OC1PE, CCER.CC1E, CR1.ARPE, and the pin's AF
DIER.UIE, SR.UIF, EGR.UG, and the pin's MODER output
CCMR1 mode, CCR1, PSC, and the NVIC enable
CCER.CC1P, CCER.CC1NP, CR1.CEN, and the pin's pull-up
why: Mode and preload in CCMR1, CC1E to connect the channel to the pin, ARPE, and the alternate function on the pin. Interrupts and NVIC are not needed for the waveform.

q: What does OC1PE (CCR1 preload) guarantee when the ISR changes the pulse width?
choices: A pulse is never cut in half: changes wait for the next frame
The pulse width changes at once, even in the middle of a pulse
The new value is ignored until software writes EGR = UG again
The output is forced low for as long as CCR1 is being written
why: With preload on, every change to CCR1 takes effect at the next update, the frame boundary, so no malformed pulse is produced.

q: TIM3 counts at 1 MHz with ARR = 19999. CCR1 = 1250. What is on PA6?
why: One count is 1 µs, so CCR1 = 1250 is 1.25 ms high, and ARR + 1 = 20 000 counts is the 20 ms frame.

q: What CCMR1 value sets OC1M = 110 (bits 6:4) and OC1PE (bit 3)?
why: 0b110 << 4 = 0x60, plus 1 << 3 = 0x08, gives 0x68. 0x60 forgets the preload.

q: What does a hobby servo read, nominally?
choices: A pulse every 20 ms: 1.0 ms one end, 1.5 ms centre, 2.0 ms other end
A pulse every 1 ms: 20 % one end, 50 % centre, 80 % other end
A pulse every 20 ms: 0 ms one end, 10 ms centre, 20 ms other end
A voltage: 0 V one end, 1.65 V centre, 3.3 V other end
why: The pulse width is the whole message; the 50 Hz frame rate is not critical. Real servos differ (Arduino uses 544–2400 µs), so the lab measures it.

q: Lab check T9: PSC is changed so TIM3 counts at 2 MHz; ARR = 19999 and CCR1 = 1500 are unchanged. What happens?
choices: 100 updates/s, and the pulse shrinks to 0.75 ms
50 updates/s, and the pulse stays 1.5 ms
25 updates/s, and the pulse grows to 3 ms
100 updates/s, and the pulse stays 1.5 ms
why: At 2 MHz the frame is 20 000 × 0.5 µs = 10 ms, so 100 updates/s, and 1500 counts are only 750 µs. CCR1 still holds the pulse width, now in half-microseconds.

q: TIM3_CH1 is AF1 on PA6. What is it on PB6?
why: AF numbers depend on the pin: TIM3_CH1 is AF1 on PA6 (and PB4, PC6) but AF12 on PB6 and AF11 on PB7. The number comes from the datasheet table.

q: Which AF connects TIM14_CH1 to PA7?
why: TIM14_CH1 is AF4 on PA7 (but AF0 on PB1).

q: TIM3 is set up correctly but PA6 is given the wrong AF number. What do you see?
choices: The timer counts and interrupts at 50/s, but the servo never moves
The timer refuses to start counting until the AF number is corrected
A HardFault occurs the first time the timer tries to drive the pin
The PWM comes out on a different pin, the one that AF belongs to
why: With a wrong AF the timer works and the pin doesn't. Everything internal looks fine, including the self-test.

q: PA6 needs AF1 and PA7 needs AF4. What does GPIOA->AFR[0] hold for just those two pins?
What does the TIM3 update ISR do with SLEW?
choices: Moves CCR1 toward the target by at most SLEW µs per frame
Sets CCR1 straight to the target, then waits SLEW µs
Skips SLEW frames between servo updates
Adds SLEW µs of dead time between pulses
why: It is a rate limiter, the smallest control loop: measure, compare, correct, once per period. The servo glides instead of snapping.

q: SLEW = 20 µs per 20 ms frame. How long does the servo take to glide from 1000 µs to 2000 µs?
why: 1000 µs / 20 µs = 50 frames, and 50 × 20 ms = 1 s: 1000 µs of travel per second.

q: Lab check T4: SERVO_SLEW_US goes from 20 to 200. How many frames from 1000 µs to 2000 µs now?
why: 1000 / 200 = 5 frames, 100 ms: the servo now nearly snaps.

q: Why measure the echo with input capture instead of an EXTI interrupt reading the time?
choices: The hardware copies CNT into CCR1 at the edge; latency doesn't matter
Capture runs from a faster clock than the EXTI block, so it is finer
EXTI cannot interrupt on both edges of the same pin, only on one
Capture needs no interrupt at all, so the CPU is never even told
why: The timestamp is taken before the interrupt is even requested; latency changes when you read it, not what it says. EXTI can do both edges; the ISR still reads CCR1.

q: How is CC1IF cleared in the capture ISR?
why: Reading CCR1 clears CC1IF: the third clearing convention, and the only one needing no write.

q: TIM14 counts µs and wraps at 65536. The rising edge is captured at 65000 and the falling at 1000. What width does (uint16_t)(t_fall − t_rise) give?
why: (1000 − 65000) mod 65536 = 1536: 536 counts to the wrap plus 1000 after. The 16-bit subtraction is right across one wrap, like millis().

q: How long until a 16-bit TIM14 counting at 1 MHz wraps?
why: 2¹⁶ µs = 65.536 ms. The longest HC-SR04 echo, 400 cm, is 23.2 ms, so at most one wrap can happen between edges.

q: TIM14 capture is configured but only CC1P is set, for rising edges. What does the report show?
choices: No widths, ever: there is no falling edge to subtract
Widths twice as long as the real echo
Correct widths, since the fall is implied
A HardFault at the first echo
why: From the silent-failure list: capture both edges, or you only ever have rising timestamps and no width.

q: The guide's figure for the HC-SR04 echo is about how much per centimetre?
why: Round-trip at ~340 m/s is ~58 µs per cm. Wokwi's model is actually 58.8 µs per cm.

q: An echo is 2900 µs wide. At 58 µs per cm, how far is the object?
Lab check T3: PING_MS goes from 100 to 50. How fast does the EXTI edge count grow now?
why: 20 pings a second, two edges per echo (rise and fall): 40 edges a second, up from 20.

q: Wokwi does not implement timer input capture. How does lesson 06 still measure the echo there?
choices: EXTI line 7 interrupts on both edges and reads TIM14->CNT itself
It polls PA7 in main() and reads millis()
It uses TIM3's capture channel instead of TIM14's
It estimates the width from the servo position
why: The handler reads TIM14->CNT on each edge. Both timestamps are late by about the same latency, so the width is still right while nothing delays one of the two interrupts.

q: The capture ISR writes echo_us and echo_count together. Why does main() read them between __disable_irq() and __enable_irq()?
choices: So a capture between the two loads can't pair a new count with an old width
Because each variable on its own could tear on a 32-bit core like this one
So that the capture itself is delayed until main() has finished reading
Because volatile variables cannot be read while interrupts are enabled
why: Each word alone is safe, but the pair is one logical value. Masking for two loads keeps the pair consistent. The capture is not delayed: the hardware already took the timestamp; the interrupt just waits pending.

q: While main() reads the pair with interrupts masked, an echo edge arrives. What happens to the measurement?
choices: It is still exact: CCR1 already holds the time
It is lost: an edge that arrives while masked is never captured
It is late by the length of the masked window, a few microseconds
It is captured twice, once now and once when interrupts are re-enabled
why: Capture is hardware; the interrupt is merely held pending until __enable_irq(). The window is two loads, a fraction of a microsecond.

q: Lesson 06 gives TIM14 capture priority 1, TIM3 update 2, SysTick 3. What rule is that?
choices: Deadline-monotonic: the shorter the deadline, the more urgent
Importance to the user: the servo matters most
IRQ number order: the lowest number is most urgent
Rate order: whoever interrupts most often is most urgent
why: Capture must be read before the next edge, TIM3 has 20 ms of slack, and a late tick is still counted. Importance to the user is not the criterion.

q: A student argues: 'the servo is what the user sees, so TIM3 should be priority 0.' What is the guide's answer?
choices: Wrong: TIM3 has 20 ms of slack; priority follows deadline
Right: the output the user can see always gets the top priority
Right: PWM must be serviced by the CPU on every edge of the pulse
Wrong: TIM3 must be the least urgent, below SysTick's priority 3
why: The CPU is in no PWM edge and the update ISR has a whole 20 ms frame. The capture read has the tightest deadline.

q: TIM3 (IRQ 16) and TIM14 (IRQ 19) are both pending at the same NVIC priority. What happens?
choices: Neither preempts; TIM3 runs first, then TIM14
TIM14 preempts TIM3, as the higher IRQ number
They run interleaved, one instruction each
why: Equal priorities never preempt each other; they queue, and the lower IRQ number goes first.

q: NVIC priority bytes hold prio << 6. What byte gives TIM14 priority 1?
why: With 2 priority bits at the top of the byte, 1 << 6 = 0x40. Priority 2 is 0x80 and 3 is 0xC0.

q: Counting TIM3 updates per SysTick second should give what number?
why: Two independent clock paths from the same 48 MHz must agree: 1 s / 20 ms = 50.

q: Lab check T8: REPORT_MS goes from 1000 to 250, and 'TIM3 n/s' now reads about 12. Is TIM3 slower?
choices: No: it counts updates per report, now a quarter second
Yes: TIM3 shares its clock with the report, so it slows down too
Yes: the report now preempts TIM3 four times as often as before
No: SysTick itself slowed down by a factor of four, not TIM3
why: The number is updates − last_updates per report interval: 50 × 0.25 ≈ 12.5. The timer is unchanged; the label says /s.

q: Forgetting the RCC clock gate for TIM3 gives which symptom?
choices: The timer counts at the reset 12 MHz
The first period is at the wrong rate
why: Without the clock gate the peripheral is unpowered: writes are lost, reads return 0. The wrong-rate first period is the missing UG.

q: PWM is configured but CCER.CC1E is never set. What happens?
choices: The timer runs but the pin is dead, as with a wrong AF
The timer does not count at all
The pin outputs a constant high
why: CC1E connects the channel to the pin. Without it the counter, the interrupt and the report all look fine and the channel never reaches the pin.

q: TIM3_IRQHandler is misspelled as TIM3_IRQhandler. What happens?
choices: The vector stays Default_Handler, and the board hangs
The linker stops with an undefined-symbol error for TIM3_IRQHandler
Nothing goes wrong: the compiler matches handler names case-insensitively
Nothing goes wrong: the NVIC finds the handler by its IRQ number
why: The handler is found by its exact name: the weak alias stays in the table and the real function is never called. It builds with no error.

q: The proximity bar lights (200 − cm) × 8 / 200 LEDs as the mask (1 << lit) − 1. Which mask at 150 cm?
In a preemptive scheduler (an RTOS), who stops a running job?
choices: The kernel, on a timer interrupt
The NVIC, when the job's priority drops
The idle task, when it becomes ready
why: Preemptive: the kernel takes the CPU away on the tick. Cooperative (the superloop): the job stops only by returning.

q: A prime-finding loop that never returns is added. What happens under each scheduler?
choices: Superloop: everything freezes. RTOS: the hog is preempted
Superloop: the hog is preempted. RTOS: everything else freezes
Both freeze, because a CPU hog takes every cycle under either scheduler
Both keep working, because SysTick still interrupts the hog in each
why: A cooperative scheduler works only while every job agrees to be short. A preemptive one stops the hog mid-calculation, without its consent, and resumes it later.

q: SysTick still interrupts during a superloop CPU hog. Does that rescue the other superloop jobs?
choices: No: the handler returns to the hog, and no job is switched
Yes: SysTick runs each of the other superloop jobs in turn
Yes: the NVIC preempts the hog once for each waiting job
No: SysTick is masked for as long as the CPU hog keeps running
why: An interrupt alone only counts time; switching to another job needs a kernel that saves one context and restores another. That is what lesson 07 adds.

q: In the measured run, the hog shows 100 % CPU while bar and button show 0 %. Why do bar and button still work?
choices: They preempt the hog within a tick, work briefly, and sleep
They run on a second core while the hog keeps the first one busy
The hog yields to them voluntarily after every prime it finds
They run inside SysTick_Handler, entirely outside the scheduler
why: Higher-priority tasks preempt the hog the moment they are ready. Their work is so short that the per-tick profile charges them 0 %.

q: What is a task's context?
choices: Its registers plus its stack pointer
Its source code together with all of its global variables
Its priority and its current state in the scheduler's lists
Its TCB together with the list of mutexes it currently holds
why: Save the context and the function can be put away; restore it and it continues as if nothing happened.

q: What is a TCB?
choices: The task control block: the kernel's record of one task
The timer control block that drives the tick
The task's copy of the core registers
The table of callbacks for each interrupt
why: os_task_t holds sp, name, prio, base_prio, state, wake and more.

q: Why must sp be the first field of the TCB?
choices: The assembly in PendSV reads it at [tcb + 0]
The C standard requires pointers to come first
The hardware loads PSP from the TCB on exception return
So the TCB is 8-byte aligned for the stack
why: PendSV_Handler is hand-written assembly that loads and stores the saved stack pointer at offset 0 of the TCB. Move the field and the switch breaks silently. The hardware knows nothing about TCBs.

q: Why does the TCB only need to remember the task's saved stack pointer?
choices: Each task's registers are saved on its own stack
The core keeps every task's registers in banked copies
Tasks never use registers other than sp
The registers are saved in a global array indexed by task
why: Each task has its own stack and its registers live there while it is switched out; the TCB just points at them.

q: How many words of context does one switched-out task keep on its stack?
why: 8 words pushed by the hardware (r0–r3, r12, lr, pc, xPSR) plus 8 saved by PendSV (r4–r11).

q: Five tasks are created. How many bytes of forged context does os_task_create write in total?
why: Each forged frame is 16 words = 64 bytes (8 for the hardware frame, 8 for r4–r11); 5 × 64 = 320.

q: Which stack pointer do exception handlers use?
why: Handlers always run on MSP. CONTROL.SPSEL = 1 only selects PSP for Thread mode.

q: When do tasks run on PSP?
why: PSP is the process stack for Thread mode when SPSEL = 1; main() after reset uses MSP.

q: Why do handlers never need room on a task's stack beyond the 8-word frame?
choices: Handlers run on MSP, a stack no task owns
Handlers are forbidden from using local variables
The NVIC allocates handler stacks in the TCB
Handlers push their registers onto PSP, then switch
why: The hardware frame goes on the interrupted task's stack; everything the handler does after that uses MSP. Each task's stack only has to hold that task.

q: What does EXC_RETURN = 0xFFFFFFFD mean?
choices: Return to Thread mode, use PSP
Return to Thread mode, use MSP
why: 0xFFFFFFFD is Thread/PSP, the value every switch in this kernel returns with. 0xFFFFFFF9 is Thread/MSP and 0xFFFFFFF1 is Handler mode.

q: What does EXC_RETURN = 0xFFFFFFF9 mean?
choices: Return to Thread mode, use MSP
Return to Thread mode, use PSP
Return to Handler mode, use MSP
A fault on the process stack
why: 0xFFFFFFF9: Thread mode on MSP, as main() uses after reset.

q: Which bit of EXC_RETURN says 'use PSP', and what is it in 0xFFFFFFF9?
why: D = 1101 has bit 2 set (PSP); 9 = 1001 has it clear (MSP). Bit 3 is the Thread/Handler bit.

q: A HardFault handler reads lr = 0xFFFFFFF1. Who faulted?
choices: main(), in Thread mode on MSP
why: 0xFFFFFFF1 is Handler mode, and its bit 2 is clear, so the frame is on MSP. A task fault would show 0xFFFFFFFD.

q: How are xPSR, MSP, PSP, PRIMASK and CONTROL reached?
choices: Only with mrs and msr: they have no memory address
With ordinary ldr and str at fixed addresses inside the SCB
With ldr and str at 0xE000E000 and the words just after it
Only from Handler mode, through a request made to the NVIC
why: They live inside the core, outside the memory map. CMSIS wraps the instructions as __get_PSP(), __set_PRIMASK() and so on.

q: A FreeRTOS port for the M3 uses BASEPRI to mask only some interrupts. What does the M0+ offer?
choices: Only PRIMASK: no BASEPRI or FAULTMASK on this core
BASEPRI as well, at exactly the same address as on the Cortex-M3
FAULTMASK, which masks every interrupt except NMI by priority
BASEPRI, but it can only be written while in Handler mode
why: The M0+ has PRIMASK alone; CMSIS compiles BASEPRI and FAULTMASK only for Thumb-2 cores.

q: What does CONTROL read while a task runs in this kernel?
why: SPSEL (bit 1) = 1 means Thread mode uses PSP. The kernel never writes CONTROL; the exception return with 0xFFFFFFFD sets SPSEL.

q: Where is the SCB, and which two of its registers does the kernel use?
why: The System Control Block is part of the core at 0xE000ED00. ICSR pends PendSV; SHPR3 holds the PendSV and SysTick priorities. 0xE000E100 is the NVIC; 0xE000E010 is SysTick.

q: ICSR is at offset 0x04 in the SCB and PENDSVSET is bit 28. What is the write that pends PendSV?
why: 1 << 28 = 0x10000000, written to 0xE000ED00 + 4. 0x08000000 is bit 27, PENDSVCLR.

q: Why is PendSV pended with SCB->ICSR = PENDSVSET and not |=?
choices: ICSR is write-1-to-act; zeros do nothing
|= would also set PENDSVCLR, which would cancel the request at once
ICSR is a write-only register, so the read in |= would fault
|= is three instructions, so an interrupt could split it and lose the bit
why: In ICSR writing 1 acts and writing 0 does nothing. A |= reads back status bits and writes them as requests, which is wrong for a write-1-to-act register.
